title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by fallout from the US midterms, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress. It covers President Trump's offer of the press secretary job to UFC chief Dana White, his call for a Justice Department probe of Democrats, and how the results could reshape AI and data-center policy. Abroad, Israel's president asked Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a government, and a gunman killed six people in Krakow, Poland.

stories.headline: Trump offers White House press secretary job to UFC chief Dana White
stories.summary: President Trump said on Truth Social on Saturday that he had offered the vacant White House press secretary job to UFC CEO Dana White, a close friend and longtime supporter. Trump asked White to bring six UFC fighters as "assistants" to "defend us against the Lunatic Left." CNN reported that White had declined and that one presidential aide called the offer a joke. White then posted a photo of himself at the briefing-room lectern captioned "On to the next chapter." Speaking in London, he said he was flying to Washington for a Monday meeting with Trump, without saying whether he would take the job.
key_facts: The press secretary post has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left in mid-October after one briefing; Karoline Leavitt had stepped down at the end of August.
Trump named six fighters as proposed aides and acknowledged some "are not from our Country"; he misspelled Kayla Harrison's name as "Harris."
White said: "I'm flying to Washington, D.C. right now" and "I have a lot of jobs already."
The offer came a day after Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, following heavy Republican midterm losses.
The White House did not respond to requests for comment on the post.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and PBS (AP) placed the offer against the GOP's midterm losses and the Miller appointment. PBS called it unconventional "even for the norm-busting president" and noted no one in the White House confirmed it. The Guardian raised the possibility that it was a stunt to change the subject. It also noted White's wealth compared with the job's $195,000 salary, Nurmagomedov's reported closeness to Putin, and Makhachev's comments on Gaza. It contrasted right-wing criticism of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for saying "Alhamdulillah" with Makhachev's use of the same phrase.

Deutsche Welle gave a straightforward account. It covered the conflicting signals from White's Instagram post and CNN's report that he declined, the turnover in the press secretary role, and the Trump–White friendship, including the UFC event on the White House lawn. The Hill mentioned it only briefly in a live blog.

The New York Post centred White's own comments that he was flying to DC and had a meeting with Trump, treating it as a developing story. The Washington Examiner quoted Trump's post and described White as a longtime ally, without commentary.

disputed: Whether White has accepted or declined: CNN reported he turned it down, but White said he would discuss it with Trump on Monday.
Whether the offer was serious; CNN cited an aide calling it a joke.
Accounts differ on Zacharia's tenure: five days (DW, AP) versus four days (New York Post).
stories.why: Who speaks for the White House shapes how the administration communicates with the press and public as it adjusts to a Democratic Congress.

stories.headline: Israel's president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to try to form a government
stories.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Saturday he would task Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who leads the opposition Yashar party, with forming a government after the October 27 election. Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's won a majority. Most parties, including two Arab-led lists, recommended Eisenkot. He will receive the mandate formally on Sunday and has 28 days to build a 61-seat majority, with a possible 14-day extension. Netanyahu called for a "national unity government" and warned against relying on what he called "terrorist supporters," his term for the Arab-led parties.
key_facts: Netanyahu's Likud won 27 seats, his bloc 53 of 120; Eisenkot's four-party bloc won 48.
Factions with 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot and 46 backed Netanyahu; United Torah Judaism's 7 members endorsed no one.
The Arab-led Joint List and Ra'am together hold 19 seats and recommended Eisenkot.
Eisenkot on X: "Now is the time to form a national emergency government."
If no one forms a government, Israel faces new elections; it held five between 2019 and 2022.

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) and The Guardian focused on the Arab-led parties as fraught potential kingmakers. AP described as unsubstantiated Netanyahu's claims that Arab parties "stole" the election. The Guardian profiled Eisenkot as "no peacenik": he opposes a Palestinian state and devised the "Dahiya doctrine," but has also vowed to crack down on violent West Bank settlers.
Axios and The Hill gave brief accounts. Axios called it the closest Netanyahu has come to losing power since 2021 and noted that deep divisions could still block a government.

Fox News detailed the seat arithmetic and stressed that 67 endorsements do not equal a 67-seat coalition, since some partners rule out relying on Arab parties. It quoted Eisenkot's four founding principles at length, including dismantling Hamas. The Washington Examiner briefly called it a setback for Netanyahu.

disputed: Whether Eisenkot's bloc will accept support from Arab-led parties, formally or from outside the coalition.
Whether a broad unity government with Likud is possible, given disputes over ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions and an October 7 inquiry.
stories.why: The outcome could end Netanyahu's long tenure and reshape Israel's approach to Gaza, the West Bank and its domestic divisions.

stories.headline: Gunman kills six in Krakow's main square; Polish leaders call it terrorism
stories.summary: A 25-year-old Polish man drove through Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon and fired an automatic weapon at random people from his car. He killed six people and wounded more than a dozen before police shot and arrested him within about three minutes. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultranationalistic" views, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the attack terrorism. Police later found the bodies of two women and a man, likely relatives, at the suspect's home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Poland will observe two days of national mourning on Sunday and Monday.
key_facts: The dead were four women and two men: three Polish women, one British national, and two not yet identified.
Five foreigners were among the injured, from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia; two police officers were seriously wounded.
The suspect wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and more weapons and ammunition were found in his car.
Authorities said he appears to have acted alone and was not a soldier; his name has not been released.
Krakow's mayor declared city mourning until Wednesday, saying "The square will belong to us again."

perspectives.framing: The Guardian ran live updates stressing the far-right motive, police heroism and Tusk's warning about online disinformation. PBS carried the AP report, which linked to a piece on hostility toward Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

Deutsche Welle and the BBC gave factual explainers. They covered casualties, the suspect's views and international condolences. The BBC added verified footage, the injured officers' names, and Polish media reports that the suspect had a gun permit.

The New York Post ran the AP report under a headline calling the gunman a "lunatic" while keeping the far-right detail. Fox News emphasised the tourist setting, Tusk's appeal to politicians not to exploit the tragedy, and police denials of false rumours. It linked to other recent attacks, including fears of copycat school attacks in Poland.

disputed: The injured count varies: 16 (DW, BBC, including the attacker) versus 15 (AP, Fox).
Whether the guns were legally held; Polish media reported he had a permit and may have taken weapons from his family home.
The full motive and the circumstances of the deaths at his home are under investigation.
AP attributes the "act of terror" description to the defence minister; other outlets quote Tusk calling it terrorism.
stories.why: Mass shootings are rare in Poland, and an apparently ideologically motivated attack is likely to shape debate over extremism and gun ownership there.

stories.headline: Trump orders Justice Department to investigate Democrats over alleged threats, naming Sen. Slotkin
stories.summary: President Trump said on Saturday he was ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democrats for "threatening" Republican officials, donors and supporters with impeachment and other punishment. He called this "extortion at the highest level" and specifically named Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin. Outlets noted that he did not identify specific communications or provide evidence of criminal conduct. The post follows Democrats' midterm wins, after which some said they would investigate Trump-family finances, ICE and cabinet officials. Neither the White House nor Slotkin immediately commented.
key_facts: Trump wrote: "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!"
Slotkin said in an October 13 speech that she wanted young people to think twice before working for the Trump administration, calling it a "deterrence message."
Slotkin was among Democrats in a November 2025 video urging troops to refuse illegal orders; a federal grand jury later declined to indict the video's participants.
Rep. Robert Garcia, likely incoming House Oversight chair, posted "LAWYER UP" after the election.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera stressed that the claims came without evidence and set them against Democrats' plans for oversight probes once they take Congress in January. It noted Trump's earlier calls to investigate critics such as James Comey and Letitia James.
CNBC noted the lack of evidence and supplied the context of Slotkin's October speech, the 2025 video dispute and the grand jury's refusal to indict. The Hill briefly reported the request.
The Washington Examiner reported the order and quoted Trump's post at length, including his claim that no impeachable acts had been committed, highlighting that he named Slotkin.

disputed: What specific "threatening letters" or communications Trump is referring to.
Whether the Justice Department will open an investigation.
stories.why: It foreshadows a confrontation between the administration and a Democratic Congress over oversight and use of federal law enforcement.

stories.headline: Reported US intelligence memo alleges Chinese spy targeted Nvidia CEO; Congress signals scrutiny
stories.summary: Media reports, led by The New York Times, say a memo based on US intelligence claimed that Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Financial Times reported that the memo also claimed the two had a romantic relationship. Nvidia said their interactions were "not unusual" and that it does not share classified information with customers. Sen. Chris Coons promised a congressional probe. Separately, a planned Seoul visit by Huang's daughter, Nvidia senior director Madison Huang, was cancelled, which sources attributed to "family issues."
key_facts: The memo circulated earlier this year, according to the reports.
A separate NYT report found only an empty shell at the listed office of New Matrix, a Chinese firm the Commerce Department authorised to buy advanced Nvidia chips.
The Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 event is expected to go ahead without Madison Huang.

perspectives.framing: All coverage came from center outlets. TechCrunch summarised the NYT and FT reports alongside Nvidia's denial. Axios emphasised Huang's global importance and likely bipartisan congressional attention. Yonhap and The Korea Herald reported the trip cancellation and noted that observers speculated about a link to the spy reports.

disputed: The memo's claims are unverified and reported second-hand.
Whether Madison Huang's cancellation is connected to the reports.
stories.why: Nvidia's chips are central to AI and US–China tech competition, so questions about its leadership's exposure to foreign intelligence carry policy weight.

stories.headline: Man charged with murder and kidnapping after Statesville death
stories.summary: Statesville, N.C., police responded to a suspicious-activity call near Museum Road and the Gregory Creek Trailhead around 7:49 p.m. on Friday and found a man with traumatic injuries. He was identified as Jason Stanley and died at a hospital. Police arrested Noah Harris, 27, and charged him with murder and first-degree kidnapping. Investigators said the two knew each other and the attack was not random.
key_facts: The victim was Jason Stanley.
The suspect, Noah Harris, 27, is charged with murder and first-degree kidnapping.
Police said the incident was not a random act of violence.

perspectives.framing: Local TV stations reported the police account without additional commentary; earlier reports described only a "person of interest."

disputed: Police have not disclosed the nature of the injuries or a motive.
stories.why: It is a local homicide case in the Charlotte area with an arrest made.

stories.headline: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas by mid-2027
stories.summary: Elon Musk said on Friday that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around mid-2027 to make room for its Cybercab robotaxi. He did not say whether the truck would be built elsewhere or what happens to outstanding orders. Sales fell far short of the planned 250,000-a-year capacity. The truck also faced recalls and build-quality complaints, and its image became tied to Musk's politics.
key_facts: Musk claimed 250,000 preorders after the 2019 unveiling; deliveries began in late 2023.
Cox Automotive estimates total sales of 72,702, more than half in 2024.
Cybercab production began in April, and paid rides started in Austin in September.

perspectives.framing: The Verge ran an opinion piece headlined "Good riddance, Cybertruck!" calling it an epic failure driven by Musk's hubris. It tied the decision to his costly losing bets on Republican candidates in the midterms and said SpaceX bought unsold trucks.

The Korea Herald, carrying AFP, gave a factual account of sales, recalls and the shift to robotaxis, quoting a Cox Automotive analyst on the truck becoming a "niche" product, and noted its political associations.

disputed: Whether the Cybertruck will be fully discontinued or built elsewhere.
Sales totals differ slightly: about 70,000 (The Verge) versus 72,702 (Cox Automotive).
stories.why: It signals Tesla's pivot from carmaking toward robotaxis, a bet that depends on unproven fully driverless technology.

stories.headline: Midterm results raise prospects for data-center limits and AI regulation
stories.summary: Coverage after the midterms argues that Democratic gains could create hurdles for the tech industry. Voters passed many local measures restricting data centers, and candidates such as Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on limiting them. TechCrunch's podcast discussed Elon Musk's large Republican donations yielding little and companies like OpenAI signalling policy changes. Vox argued that the bigger story is the election of candidates focused on AI safety who may push broader regulation.
key_facts: Vox reports 40 ballot measures to slow or stop data centers passed.
In an exit poll cited by Vox, 56% said AI and data centers were a "crucial or a major factor" in their congressional vote.
TechCrunch says Musk donated roughly half a billion dollars to Republicans.

perspectives.framing: Vox framed data centers as a gateway issue. It emphasised newly elected AI-safety-minded figures such as Abdul El-Sayed, Jon Ossoff and Scott Wiener, and Sen. Maria Cantwell's framework, arguing that regulating the technology itself matters more.

TechCrunch focused on business implications: roadblocks for data centers, especially in Texas, Musk's political setback and industry adjustment. Its hosts debated whether tech is overly focused on the issue.

disputed: How much anti-data-center and AI sentiment drove the Democratic wave; TechCrunch hosts said it was probably not the main cause.
stories.why: New lawmakers and local rules could slow the AI infrastructure buildout and shape how the technology is regulated.

stories.headline: Charlotte holds Veterans Day parade and festival
stories.summary: Charlotte held its annual Salute to Veterans Parade in Uptown on Saturday, drawing more than 2,000 people, according to Queen City News. A nonprofit also hosted the Carolinas Veterans Day Festival at Romare Bearden Park, highlighting veteran-owned businesses and employer resources. The events open a week of observances ahead of Veterans Day on Wednesday.
key_facts: More than 2,000 people attended, per Queen City News.
Veterans Day falls on Wednesday.

perspectives.framing: Local stations covered it as a community event, noting bands, scouts, vendors and veteran resources.

stories.why: It is a local community observance, with more events planned through the week.

stories.headline: K-dramas and K-pop drive tourism growth in South Korea
stories.summary: CNA reports that fans of Korean dramas and K-pop are travelling to South Korea to visit filming locations, rent hanbok and try temple stays. Busan saw a surge in foreign visitors, helped by a BTS concert in June. The report notes the benefits have not been spread evenly.
key_facts: A record 55,515 foreigners did temple stays last year; about one in 10 identified as Buddhist.
Busan had more than 3.4 million foreign visitors from January to August, up 46% year on year.
Paradise Hotel Busan said foreign guests rose to about 70% during the BTS concert dates.

perspectives.framing: CNA wrote a feature built on tourist interviews and tourism statistics, noting that some local vendors saw little benefit.

stories.why: It shows how cultural exports can boost tourism and regional economies, including areas facing population decline.
